# Meet the Hosts: ACLU Launches New Podcast 'Let the Record Show'


Hosts Shereen Marisol Meraji and Matthew Beat give a glimpse into the ACLU’s new podcast covering some of the most influential court cases in history.


[Hibah Ansari](https://www.aclu.org/bios/hibah-ansari) ,
she/her/hers


,
ACLU


**Share This Page**


September 23, 2026


As a journalist and educator, Shereen Marisol Meraji spends a lot of time thinking about how to help people understand complicated things — without the jargon. The same applies when talking about constitutional law. “Legalese” is another language altogether, but it shouldn’t deter people from understanding the court’s decisions throughout history.


About a thousand miles away from her is Matthew Beat, a former history teacher who spends much of his time on YouTube. He’s the creator behind several viral videos that explain some of the world’s most complex issues. Together, Meraji and Beat form the duo that lend their voice to[“Let the Record Show,”](https://www.aclu.org/podcast) the ACLU’s newest podcast.


What Happens When the President Defies a Judge?


What Happens When the President Defies a Judge?


[Visit this episode](https://www.aclu.org/podcast/what-happens-when-the-president-defies-a-judge)


“When the ACLU came to me with this idea, I loved it immediately. I thought, ‘Oh, this could be really fun,’” Meraji said. “We can tell these incredible stories and make constitutional law feel accessible, not like you’re sitting in a law school classroom, but like you’re hanging out with two of your favorite nerdy friends.”


In a country where threats to civil liberties have begun to feel increasingly overwhelming, “Let the Record Show” invites listeners to take a beat and look back.


“Let the Record Show” is a new, irreverent American history podcast that looks back on the people and places behind defining legal moments for rights and freedoms in the United States. On every episode, our hosts explore a major court case from U.S. history. Cases that shape how we live our lives today. And it’s more than just the case and its outcome — it’s about the people and places beyond the courtroom, and the moments that came to define our country’s complex system of laws.


“Matt and I come at these stories from different places, which is part of what makes it fun. He’s a history teacher, and I’m a journalist,” Meraji said. “Matt is really good at taking us back in time and helping us understand the world these cases came from. And I’m often asking: What part of this story got left out of the mainstream historical record — and why? And how does this history help us understand the news today?”


Expect to experience much more than stuffy old case law. Listeners will hear about the people, places and narratives behind the cases; the captivating, bizarre and nail-biting moments in American history; and the ACLU’s long track record of going toe to toe with the government.


At the core of our show are the hosts, Meraji and Beat: two sharp and witty history nerds who inject bold humor, intrigue, and compelling commentary along the way. On “Let the Record Show,” Meraji and Beat will be joined by ACLU spokespeople, legal advocates, experts from partner organizations, and other surprise guests all weighing in on American civics.


“We joke, we get angry, we get sad, we get inspired. That’s good because that means the fire is burning,” Beat said. “Shereen is just so darn easy to get along with. She’s wise and passionate, and I learn so much from her. She even pretends to laugh at my bad jokes!”


## Shereen Marisol Meraji


Credit: LaQuann Dawson


Shereen Marisol Meraji is an associate professor and the head of the audio journalism concentration at UC Berkeley’s Graduate School of Journalism. She is an award-winning audio journalist known for her expertise in race and identity reporting, and a leader in shaping inclusive practices in public media and journalism education.


Meraji is best known as the co-founder, senior producer, and former co-host of NPR’s “Code Switch,” a groundbreaking podcast that explores race and identity in the United States. During her tenure, “Code Switch” became a national touchstone, used by educators, scholars, and media institutions to inform and deepen conversations about systemic racism. In 2020, Apple Podcasts named Code Switch its first-ever Show of the Year.


At UC Berkeley, Meraji brings over two decades of field experience into the classroom, designing curriculum that merges technical training in audio storytelling with critical insights into how race, representation, and power shape the news. She launched the J-school’s first-ever foundational reporting course in audio. Meraji’s current research and creative work continue to focus on racial and gender equity.


Meraji wants listeners to know that rights can feel permanent once we have them, but “Let the Record Show” shows how much the constitutional protections we take for granted were not inevitable.


“You look back and think, ‘Well, of course women should be allowed to serve on juries,’ or ‘Of course undocumented children should be able to attend public school,’” Meraji said. “But then you actually go back and look at these cases and realize: No. People fought over this. And, things could have gone very differently.”


## Matthew Beat, Known As Mr. Beat


Credit: LaQuann Dawson


Beat is a multifaceted creator from Kansas: a YouTuber, video producer, educator, and musician. With experience teaching a range of middle school and high school subjects, Beat has expanded his classroom to global audience through YouTube. His channel has 1.4 million subscribers and more than 370 million views. He was also named the Dole Institute of Politics Spring Fellow in 2025.


“I love the American judicial system and am fascinated by its history. I love teaching people about how our country’s legal system works, especially to an audience that often is bewildered by it,” Beat said.


While his specialty is American history, Matt is also passionate about geography, economics, and politics. Beat hopes that readers don’t feel daunted by the cases discussed in the podcast. He said each episode breaks down the case without oversimplifying the subject.


“I’m most excited about the *Engel v. Vitale* episode,” Beat said. “This *Engel* episode clears up why the mixing of religion and government is so problematic.”


## A Look Into Our First Episode


[For our series premiere](https://www.aclu.org/podcast/what-happens-when-the-president-defies-a-judge) , “Let the Record Show” will cover[J.G.G. v. Trump](https://www.aclu.org/cases/j-g-g-v-trump) , an ongoing emergency lawsuit we filed in federal court to halt removals under the Alien Enemies Act. This case now focuses in part on accountability — specifically, whether Trump officials will face consequences for openly defying a federal judge. The episodes will help make sense of our system of checks and balances.

### Daves v. Mosley


Section 131 of the newly enacted Enhance Law Enforcement Integrity Act gives Coloradans a cause of action to seek damages or equitable relief when state or local police officers violate the Colorado Constitution. In 2022, Christopher Mosley sued Officer Brendan Daves for conducting a warrantless search of his car, which Daves argued was lawful under the federal protective sweep doctrine. After Mosley prevailed at trial and the court of appeals affirmed, Daves appealed to the Colorado Supreme Court. The ACLU’s State Supreme Court Initiative and the ACLU of Colorado filed an amicus brief agreeing with Mosley’s argument that Daves has misapprehended the federal doctrine whilst focusing on a separate point: the Court’s interpretation of Section 131 is not bound by federal law.

### ACLU Celebrates the Legacy of Dolores Huerta


NEW YORK – The American Civil Liberties Union celebrates the legacy of Dolores Huerta, who passed away today at the age of 96. Huerta was one of the most influential workers’ rights leaders of the 20th century. Anthony D. Romero, ACLU executive director, had the following reaction to today’s news: “Dolores Huerta spent her life challenging injustice in every form – fighting for workers’ rights, women’s rights, immigrants’ rights, and so much more. Her bravery, perseverance, and compassion changed this country for the better. “As co-founder of the United Farm Workers Union, she successfully organized farmworker walkouts and consumer boycotts to demand better working conditions for Latino farmworkers. Today, millions of workers enjoy the protections that Ms. Huerta, and thousands of others who marched and mobilized alongside her, fought so hard to win. “The ACLU was proud to honor Ms. Huerta with the ACLU’s Roger N. Baldwin Medal of Liberty in 1993, recognizing her lifetime contributions to civil rights and civil liberties. More than three decades later, her continued legacy of standing up to injustice has stood the test of time. History will remember Dolores Huerta as a modern-day trailblazer for our rights and freedoms, and the ACLU will continue the fight to protect the justice and freedoms she spent her life working to achieve.”

### People v. Taylor


In 2013, Michigan passed the Michigan Indigent Defense Commission Act (MIDCA) to ensure that indigent criminal defendants—that is, those who cannot afford to pay for counsel themselves—received constitutionally adequate counsel, paid for by the state. This case concerns whether and under what circumstances trial courts can, consistent with MIDCA, order indigent criminal defendants to pay the state back for their attorneys. The ACLU’s State Supreme Court Initiative, the ACLU of Michigan, and the Michigan State Planning Body filed an amicus brief in the Michigan Supreme Court arguing that MIDCA, properly construed, partially abrogated a different statute authorizing trial courts to assess attorney fees against indigent defendants and explaining that allowing such orders would undermine Michiganders’ right to counsel.


**Status:** Ongoing

### ACLU Voter Education Fund and ACLU of Georgia Launch $250K Campaign to Educate Georgia Voters Ahead of Midterms


ATLANTA – The ACLU of Georgia and the ACLU Voter Education Fund are spending $250,000 in select Georgia House races to inform voters that their civil rights and liberties, including voting rights and abortion, are on the ballot this November. The ACLU Voter Education Fund will send over 225,000 mail pieces to educate voters about candidates in State House Districts 48, 53, and 105. These state races include communities like Lawrenceville, Peachtree Corners, and Sandy Springs and are highly contested. The ACLU Voter Education Fund is investing in these races because the elected candidates will influence civil rights and liberties statewide for at least two years. Their decisions will affect voting rights, reproductive rights, privacy, and other fundamental liberties. On the voter guides, residents will see candidates’ responses to questions about those issues, such as whether they would vote to repeal Georgia’s six-week abortion ban or whether they will work to prevent unnecessary restrictions on early and absentee voting. “Georgia voters have a right to know the positions that the candidates take on the rights and freedoms that shape their lives,” said Christopher Bruce, deputy executive director, ACLU of Georgia. “We’re making sure voters get the information they need to understand the issues in these elections and what the candidates would do if they had the power of the Georgia House. From reproductive freedom and voting rights to safeguarding privacy and other liberties, the choices made under the Gold Dome can have a lasting impact on our communities.” While the ACLU Voter Education Fund does not endorse or oppose any candidates, the six-figure campaign will educate voters about the candidates’ positions on key civil rights issues, including abortion, birth control, marriage equality, and voting rights for Indigenous communities, through direct mail, radio ads, and digital ads.
